item.title: Green Border (Zielona granica) with Agnieszka Holland — Jul 31
item.description:
Friday, July 31, 2026
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 2h 32m
2023 | 152 min. | Poland, France, Czechia, Belgium | Black-and-white | Polish, Arabic, English, French with English subtitles | Not Rated | DCP DIRECTED BY: Agnieszka Holland PRODUCED BY: Fred Bernstein, Agnieszka Holland, Marcin Wierzchoslawski WRITTEN BY: Maciej Pisuk, Gabriela Łazarkiewicz-Sieczko, Agnieszka Holland WITH: Jalal Altawil, Maja Ostaszewska, Behi Djanati Atai, Tomasz Włosok
Type: Screenings
Winner of the Special Jury Prize at the 2023 Venice Film Festival, Holland’s “angry and urgent masterpiece” (The Guardian) centers around the 2021 migrant crisis that unfolded in the exclusion zone between Poland and Belarus. Named for the swamplands that cover the region, Holland’s impactful narrative was conceived by reflecting on actual events, using interviews with real border guards and refugees to inform the four interwoven stories that supply the work with its incredible emotional depth. Made with trusted collaborators, including cinematographer Tomasz Naumiuk and co-writer Gabriela Łazarkiewicz-Sieczko, Green Border insists on depicting regional upheaval and conflict by prioritizing its human impact. Tim Grieson, senior US film critic for Screen International, moderates.

item.title: Europa Europa in 35mm with Agnieszka Holland — Aug 1
item.description:
Saturday, August 1, 2026
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 1h 52m
1990 | 112 min. | Germany, France, Poland | Color | German, Russian, Polish, Hebrew with English subtitles | Rated R | 35mm DIRECTED/WRITTEN BY: Agnieszka Holland PRODUCED BY: Artur Brauner, Margaret Ménégoz WITH: Marco Hofschneider, André Wilms, Ashley Wanninger, Klaus Abramowsky Print courtesy of the Joe Dante and Jon Davison Collection at the Academy Film Archive.
Type: Screenings
Inspired by the memoirs of Solomon Perel, a German Jew who evaded Nazi persecution by joining their ranks, Holland’s WWII–era biopic offers "new immediacy to the outrage by locating specific, wrenching details that transcend cliché" (New York Times). Nominated for Best Adapted Screenplay at the 64th Oscars—the film was shut out of the then-named Foreign Language Film category when Germany refused to nominate it for its thematic content—Holland’s complicated work investigates ways that denial and untruths can lead to irrepressible personal, generational, and cultural anguish. Producer Mark Johnson moderates.

item.title: Franz with Agnieszka Holland — Aug 1
item.description:
Saturday, August 1, 2026
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 2h 7m
2025 | 127 min. | Czechia, Poland, Germany, France, Turkey | Color, Black-and-white | German, Czech, Yiddish, English, French, Japanese with English subtitles | Not Rated | DCP DIRECTED BY: Agnieszka Holland PRODUCED BY: Šárka Cimbalová, Agnieszka Holland WRITTEN BY: Marek Epstein WITH: Peter Kurth, Daniel Dongres, Idan Weiss, Aaron Friesz
Type: Screenings
The life of German-speaking Jewish-Czech modernist author Franz Kafka, who died in 1924 at 40 after publishing three novels and a handful of short stories and parables, was a natural story for Holland to adapt into a film: she read his famous Metamorphosis when she was 14 and felt “since that time, Kafka is my brother” (Screen Daily). Wanting to give the character “light—and some punk infusion,” Holland takes a playful approach to the author’s idiosyncratic personality through “some kind of biography” that she hopes appeals to young people who might not be familiar with this man, who has been written about far more voluminously than he was able to write about himself. Filmmaker Jeremy Kagan moderates.

item.title: Who Framed Roger Rabbit in Dolby Vision — Aug 1
item.description:

1988. 107 min. USA. Color. English. Rated PG. DCP. Dolby Vision DIRECTED BY: Robert Zemeckis WRITTEN BY: Jeffrey Price, Peter S. Seaman WITH: Bob Hoskins, Christopher Lloyd, Joanna Cassidy, Charles Fleischer
Type: Screenings
Eddie Valiant (Bob Hoskins), a private eye in 1930s Los Angeles, gets an unexpected client—Roger Rabbit, a cartoon film star. Director Robert Zemeckis’s witty comedy-mystery is a dazzling mix of live-action and animation, incorporating beloved cartoon characters from Disney and other studios. Nominated for its art direction, cinematography, and sound, it won for its film editing, sound effects editing, and visual effects. Richard Williams also received a Special Achievement Award from the Academy for his animation direction.

item.title: Korczak with Agnieszka Holland — Aug 2
item.description:
Sunday, August 2, 2026
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 1h 58m
1990 | 118 min | Poland, Germany, United Kingdom, France | Black-and-white | Polish, German with English subtitles | Not Rated | DCP DIRECTED BY: Andrzej Wajda PRODUCED BY: Janusz Morgenstern, Willi Segler, Daniel Toscan du Plantier, Regina Ziegler WRITTEN BY: Agnieszka Holland WITH: Wojciech Pszoniak, Ewa Dałkowska, Teresa Budzisz-Krzyżanowska, Marzena Trybala
Type: Screenings
Just after Agnieszka Holland completed film school in Prague, Polish filmmaker Andrzej Wajda, already an established and celebrated auteur for films like Ashes and Diamonds (1958), welcomed the young aspirant to visit his set of The Wedding (1973). Over time, Holland said, “our relation moved from ‘master–pupil’ to something much more equal in collaboration and friendship,” and she started to write scripts with him. One of their most meaningful collaborations was this 1990 biopic about the extraordinary Polish-Jewish humanitarian Janusz Korczak, remembered “for his pedagogical philosophy and his heroic actions during the Holocaust,” Holland told the BFI. With stunning cinematography by Robby Müller (Dead Man, 1995), Korczak is, as Steven Spielberg once wrote, "one of the most important European pictures about the Holocaust." Writer and literary curator Louise Steinman moderates.

1985 | 162 min. | USA | Color | English | Rated PG | 35mm DIRECTED BY: Sydney Pollack WRITTEN BY: Kurt Leudtke WITH: Robert Redford, Meryl Streep, Klaus Maria Brandauer, Michael Kitchen Print courtesy of the Academy Film Archive.
Type: Screenings
The memoir of Danish author Karen Blixen (published under her pen name Isak Dinesen) was adapted by director Sydney Pollack and screenwriter Kurt Leudtke for this lavish romantic drama, focusing on the years Blixen (Best Actress nominee Meryl Streep) spent running a coffee farm in Nairobi and her relationship with hunter Denys Finch-Hatton (Robert Redford). Out of Africa was nominated for 11 Oscars and won seven including Best Picture, Directing (both for Pollack), Adapted Screenplay, Art Direction, Cinematography and Sound, with John Barry winning his fourth Oscar for an achingly romantic score.

item.title: The Cat Returns — Aug 3
item.description:
Monday, August 3, 2026 at 2:30 pm
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 1h 15m
2002 | 75 min. | Japan | Color | Japanese with English subtitles | Rated G | DCP DIRECTED BY: Hiroyuki Morita WRITTEN BY: Reiko Yoshida WITH: Chizuru Ikewaki, Yoshihiko Hakamada, Aki Maeda, Takayuki Yamada
Type: Screenings
A spin-off of Whisper of the Heart, The Cat Returns finds another schoolgirl encountering a mysterious tomcat on the street, though this time she is led to a fantastic world beyond her wildest dreams. Launched into a cobblestoned magic kingdom ruled by cat royalty—including a motorcade replete with vassals, maidens, and even Secret Service—she must enlist the help of the elusive Baron Humbert von Gikkingen (the same cat featured as a statue in Whisper of the Heart) if she hopes to make it back home. The only feature film directed by Hiroyuki Morita to date, The Cat Returns is a feline flight of fancy.

item.title: A Man Escaped in 35mm — Aug 3
item.description:

1956 | 101 min. | France | Black-and-White | French, German | Not Rated | 35mm DIRECTED/WRITTEN BY: Robert Bresson WITH: François Leterrier, Charles Le Clainche, Maurice Beerblock, Roland Monod
Type: Screenings
“On one side, thick walls, bars, soldiers, weapons. On the other, one lone man, unarmed, doomed from the start.” In minimalist Robert Bresson’s 1956 film, a French Resistance fighter attempts escape from a German military prison against impossible odds. While the title of the film seems to say it all, it belies the film’s gripping tension and near-silent sequences of harrowing engineering feats, unbelievable patience, and human resilience, all performed with placid determination by François Leterrier as he embodies lieutenant Fontaine, a proxy for André Devigny, whose life Bresson loosely adapted for the screen from his 1956 memoir.

item.title: Titicut Follies in 4K — Aug 5
item.description:
In person: film editor Kate Amend Selected by the Documentary Branch
Wednesday, August 5, 2026 at 7:30 pm
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 1h 27m
1967 | 87 min. | USA | Black-and-White | English | 4K DCP DIRECTED BY: Frederick Wiseman
Type: Screenings
Filmmaker Frederick Wiseman spent 29 days in 1966 at the Bridgewater State Hospital in Massachusetts, filming the treatment and mistreatment of its patients. After a year of editing, the result, the first feature from the noted documentarian, established his distinctively observational filmmaking style. Banned from public exhibition for decades and finally approved for release on First Amendment grounds in a 1991 court decision, Titicut Follies was selected for preservation by the National Film Registry in 2022. In 2016, Wiseman—whose other classic documentaries include High School (1968), Primate (1974) and Welfare (1975)— received an honorary Oscar for his “masterful and distinctive documentaries [that] examine the familiar and reveal the unexpected.”

Type: Screenings
Jane Campion’s gritty erotic thriller stars Meg Ryan as Frannie Avery, a seemingly apathetic writer and English teacher who finds solace in her daydream of language and literature. At a bar near her apartment, Frannie accidentally witnesses a sexual encounter between a woman and a man whose face she cannot recall. The woman is later found dismembered, spurring a visit from a detective who quickly becomes Frannie’s infatuation. Paralleling the desolate ambience of the urban landscape is Frannie’s facade, until her suppressed emotions trigger outbursts that may lead her straight into the path of a serial killer of women.

item.title: Basic Instinct in 4K — Aug 7
item.description:
Friday, August 7, 2026 at 7:30 pm
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 2h 7m
1992 | 127 min. | USA | Color | Scope | English | Not Rated | 4K DCP DIRECTED BY: Paul Verhoeven WRITTEN BY: Joe Eszterhas WITH: Michael Douglas, Sharon Stone, George Dzundza, Jeanne Tripplehorn
Type: Screenings
Hardboiled San Francisco detective Nick Curran (Michael Douglas) is assigned to the case of a murdered rock star and gets in over his head when he meets the victim’s lover, Catherine Tramell (Sharon Stone). A crime novelist whose latest work mirrors Curran’s case, and past relationships with violent people, Catherine becomes the prime suspect. Confronted by Tramell’s smoldering sensuality and mysterious past, Curran struggles to maintain his professionalism and not give into his carnal instincts. Paul Verhoeven’s erotic thriller made a huge impact, serving as a pop-culture reference for many years and defining the genre for the 1990s. The recipient of Academy Award nominations for editing (Frank J. Urioste) and Jerry Goldsmith’s original score, Basic Instinct, originally edited for sexual and violent content, has been restored in 4K and is now available in Verhoeven’s original, uncut version.

item.title: Harriet the Spy in 4K — Aug 8
item.description:
Saturday, August 8, 2026 at 11 am
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 1h 40m
1996 | 100 min. | USA | Color | English | Rated PG | 4K DCP DIRECTED BY: Bronwen Hughes WRITTEN BY: Douglas Petrie, Theresa Rebeck. WITH: Michelle Trachtenberg, Rosie O’Donnell, Vanessa Lee Chester, Gregory Smith
Type: Screenings
The first motion picture produced by Nickelodeon is also Bronwen Hughes’s feature film directorial debut, starring Michelle Trachtenberg as a 12-year-old Harriet Welsch, who devotes her time spying on everyone and recording her discreet detective work in a “PRIVATE” notebook. When those secrets get exposed, Harriet finds her entire class against her, including her two best friends. This sweet drama boldly and candidly surveys the bittersweet pre-teen years as an exploration of self, complementing the confusion that marks this transitional phase with Harriet’s unapologetic, cheeky spirit, letting her fight her own battles and attain redemption.

item.title: Popcorn Disabilities Conversation and Book Signing with Kristen Lopez — Aug 8
item.description:
Journalist, author, and disability advocate Kristen Lopez signs copies of her book, Popcorn Disabilities: The Highs and Lows of Disabled Representation in the Movies.
Saturday, August 8, 2026 at 2 pm
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Type: Book Signings, Conversations
Join journalist, author and disability advocate Kristen Lopez as she speaks with particular authority on how disability is represented—and too often misrepresented—in movies. It’s all examined in her book, Popcorn Disabilities: The Highs and Lows of Disabled Representation in the Movies. Lopez appears for a free conversation as well as a separate, ticketed signing of Popcorn Disabilities. Popcorn Disabilities is Lopez’s impassioned, yet fun and engaging survey of how Hollywood has dealt with disability over the last century. She reveals that, even when they're not just narrative props to help an able-bodied protagonist, movie characters with disabilities are overwhelmingly white, affluent, and conventionally attractive, obscuring the variety of disabilities and the experiences of those who deal with them. But she also explains where films have gotten it right, and how the power of the medium can enlighten and educate in the future. From little-remembered gems such as Tod Browning's Freaks (1932)—one of the earliest attempts to show dimensionality in characters with disabilities—to contemporary films such as CODA (2021), My Left Foot (1989), A Different Man (2024), and many others, it challenges popular assumptions about disability while never losing sight of movies' unique power, influence, and potential as a tool for social good.

item.title: Fritz Lang’s M — Aug 8
item.description:
In person: Academy Governor Howard A. Rodman
Saturday, August 8, 2026 at 2:30 pm
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 1h 51m
1931 | 111 min. | Germany | Black and white | German | PG-13 | DCP DIRECTED BY: Fritz Lang WRITTEN BY: Fritz Lang, Thea von Harbou WITH: Peter Lorre, Otto Wernickle, Inge Landgut, Gustaf Gründgens
Type: Screenings
One of the most influential filmmakers—whose innovative cinematic language led to such groundbreaking films such as Metropolis (1927) and Woman in the Moon (1929) —is Austrian-born Fritz Lang, who contributed to the premise of sci-fi and noir film domains in American cinema. Lang’s first sound film, M, is set in a 1930s Berlin disrupted by a gruesome serial murder case targeting children. Peter Lorre stars as the creepy murderer, Hans Beckert, who embodies the instability and confusing socio-political shifts that the nation was facing in the early 1930s. Pursued by the city police and criminals from the underworld, Beckert’s heightened anxiety is manifested through an array of daring close-up shots in high-contrast, stark, black-and-white cinematography, an apparent heir of Lang’s early work in German Expressionism.

item.title: The 4th Man in 35mm — Aug 8
item.description:
Saturday, August 8, 2026 at 7:30 pm
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 1h 42m
1983 | 102 min. | Netherlands | Color | Dutch with English subtitles | Not Rated | 35mm DIRECTED BY: Paul Verhoeven WRITTEN BY: Gerard Soeteman WITH: Jeroen Krabbé, Renée Soutendijk, Thom Hoffman, Dolf de Vries Print courtesy of the ConstellationCenter Collection at the Academy Film Archive.
Type: Screenings
In Paul Verhoeven’s stylish, psychological-erotic thriller, author Gerard (Jeroen Krabbé), begins a romantic affair with Christine (Renée Soutendijk), an enigmatic widow from literary society, only to become obsessed with her lover, Herman (Thom Hoffman). While continuing the affair in hopes of getting closer to Herman, Gerard is plagued by ominous visions, fueling paranoid thoughts about Christine plotting murder. Based on the novel by celebrated Dutch author Gerard Reve, The 4th Man was Verhoeven’s final film shot in Dutch before directing English-language and Hollywood productions. It was the Netherlands’ official submission for International Feature Film at the 56th Academy Awards, and, upon its release in the US, gave American audiences a taste of Verhoeven’s unabashed take on sex, violence, and religion.

item.title: The Thin Red Line in 35mm — Aug 9
item.description:
Sunday, August 9, 2026 at 2 pm
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 2h 45m
1998 | 165 min. | USA | Color | Scope | English | Rated R | 35mm DIRECTED/WRITTEN BY: Terrence Malick WITH: Sean Penn, Adrien Brody, Jim Caviezel, Ben Chaplin Print courtesy of the Academy Film Archive.
Type: Screenings
Terrence Malick adapted James Jones’s 1962 novel, inspired by the author’s experiences serving in World War II’s Guadalcanal campaign, for his first film since his 1978 classic Days of Heaven. Malick assembled an all-star cast (including George Clooney, Nick Nolte and John Travolta) for his unusually contemplative war epic, which received seven Oscar nominations including Directing, Adapted Screenplay (both for Malick) and Best Picture. Nominated composer Hans Zimmer spent nine months working on his evocative score, which he termed the most challenging assignment of his career.

item.title: Bunny Lake Is Missing in 4K — Aug 9
item.description:
Sunday, August 9, 2026 at 2:30 pm
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 1h 47m
1965 | 107 min. | USA | Black-and-White | English | Not Rated | 4K DCP DIRECTED BY: Otto Preminger. WRITTEN BY: John Mortimer, Penelope Mortimer WITH: Laurence Olivier, Carol Lynley, Keir Dullea, Noël Coward.
Type: Screenings
One of the most important auteurs of the 20th century cinema, Otto Preminger is known for his bold exploration of themes challenging the societal norms of his era. Carol Lynley, in an exceptional performance, portrays Ann Lake, a mother recently moved to London from New York with her 4-year-old daughter, Bunny. When Bunny vanishes without a trace, as if she never existed in the first place, Superintendent Newhouse excavates disturbing truths behind a family’s refined façade. Preminger finesses a subtle construction of atmospheric tension, amplified with a crisp, black-and-white cinematography that articulates Ann’s psychological isolation and creates an eerie, claustrophobic ambience.

item.description:

2016 | 130 min. | France/Germany | Color | Scope | French | Rated R | DCP DIRECTED BY: Paul Verhoeven WRITTEN BY: David Birke WITH: Isabelle Huppert, Laurent Lafitte, Anne Consigny, Charles Berling
Type: Screenings
Michèle (Isabelle Huppert), the head of a popular video game company, is attacked in her home by a masked assailant. Unaware of her attacker’s identity and suspicious of the men in her life, she begins to track down the criminal herself, stepping into a dangerous game of cat and mouse. Based on the award-winning novel Oh... by Philippe Djian and propelled by Huppert’s Oscar-nominated performance, Paul Verhoeven’s first French-language film was France’s official submission for International Feature Film for the 89th Academy Awards.

An adaptation of Diana Wynne Jones’s fantasy novel of the same name, the Oscar-nominated Howl’s Moving Castle is a pitch-perfect fairy tale about aging and war, set in a dazzling steampunk world. When young hatmaker Sophie is transformed into a 90-year-old woman by the vengeful Witch of the Waste, she seeks to break the curse with the help of the enigmatic wizard Howl, the fire demon Calcifer, and the magical moving castle they inhabit.

Type: Screenings
Two illusionists compete at the turn of the 20th century to create history’s greatest magic trick in this time-fracturing thriller from director/co-writer Christopher Nolan. Based on the 1995 novel by Christopher Priest, the film earned Oscar nominations for its cinematography (Wally Pfister) and art direction (Nathan Crowley, Julie Ochipinti), which cleverly used surviving Los Angeles picture palaces as key locations. The stellar cast includes Hugh Jackman and Christian Bale as the rivals, Michael Caine as their mentor, Scarlett Johansson and Rebecca Hall as the women in their lives, and a memorable cameo from David Bowie as the inventor Nikola Tesla.

item.description:
Selected by the Executives Branch
Wednesday, August 12, 2026 at 7:30 pm
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures

1942 | 100 min. | USA | Black-and-White | English | DCP DIRECTED BY: Ernst Lubitsch WRITTEN BY: Edwin Justus Mayer STORY BY: Melchior Lengyel WITH: Carole Lombard, Jack Benny, Robert Stack, Felix Bressart
Type: Screenings
A Shakespearean actor reluctantly joins a Resistance plot against the Nazis in 1939 Warsaw in this daring comedy directed by two-time Oscar nominee Ernst Lubitsch (Heaven Can Wait, 1943). Comedy legend Jack Benny had his greatest screen role as the pompous ham Joseph Tura, and Oscar nominee Carole Lombard (My Man Godfrey, 1936) was his expert match as his actress wife, Maria, her final film role before her death weeks before the film’s release. Finding the perfect balance between wartime tension and hilarious farce, Lubitsch’s classic— filmed right as the U.S. entered World War II— was remade in 1983, with Mel Brooks and Anne Bancroft as the couple.

item.title: Fatal Attraction with Adrian Lyne — Aug 13
item.description:
In person: director Adrian Lyne

1987 | 119 min. | USA | Color | English | Rated R | 4K DCP DIRECTED BY: Adrian Lyne WRITTEN BY: James Dearden WITH: Michael Douglas, Glenn Close, Anne Archer, Ellen Hamilton Latzen
Type: Screenings
Adrian Lyne’s groundbreaking 1987 erotic thriller, which garnered six Oscar nominations, contributed to the phenomenal boom of this subgenre, and it remains iconic and timeless. Glenn Close is compelling in her portrayal of Alex, a book editor who has an affair with Dan (Michael Douglas), a happily married attorney whose life becomes an unbearable torture after the tryst. Passion turns into obsession; Alex not only terrorizes Dan but also his wife and young daughter. Close’s deep dive into Alex’s psychological state, exhibited in the extreme measures she takes to possess Dan, is manifested in an intense performance,and the chemistry she shares with Douglas’s riveting Dan creates simultaneously repulsive and magnetic dynamics between them. Maya Montañez Smukler, head of the UCLA Film & Television Archive Research and Study Center, moderates.

item.description:
In person: director Adrian Lyne
Friday, August 14, 2026 at 7:30 pm
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 2h 4m
2002 | 124 min. | USA | Color | English | Rated R | 35mm DIRECTED BY: Adrian Lyne WRITTEN BY: Alvin Sargent, William Broyles, Jr. WITH: Diane Lane. Richard Gere. Olivier Martinez, Erik Per Sullivan Print courtesy of the Academy Film Archive.
Type: Screenings
Diane Lane received an Oscar nomination for her remarkable portrayal of Connie Sumner, who lives an admirable life in an upper-class neighborhood of upstate New York with loving husband Edward and 8-year-old son Charlie. In a gush of wind, an unpredictable encounter occurs between Connie and an attractive man in the street of New York City, followed by the irreversible measures of an illicit affair. Adrian Lyne candidly and without judgment surveys on lust, passion, jealousy, and guilt, unearthing a dark, dense pool of human emotion and the arbitrariness of its motivation. Karina Longworth moderates.

item.title: Scooby-Doo in 35mm — Aug 15
item.description:
Saturday, August 15, 2026 at 11 am
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Runtime: 1h 26m
2002 | 86 min. | USA | Color | English | Rated PG | 35mm DIRECTED BY: Raja Gosnell WRITTEN BY: James Gunn STORY BY: Craig Titley, James Gunn WITH: Freddie Prinze Jr., Sarah Michelle Gellar, Matthew Lillard, Linda Cardellini
Type: Screenings
The Mystery Inc. gang from Hanna-Barbera’s classic cartoon, Scooby-Doo, Where Are You! took their sleuthing skills to the big screen with their first live-action adventure in 2002’s Scooby-Doo. Led by ‘90s teen heartthrobs and real-life couple Freddie Prinze Jr. and Sarah Michelle Gellar as Fred and Daphne, the amateur detectives Velma (Linda Cardellini), Shaggy (Matthew Lillard) and his best friend, the cowardly, always hungry, and vocal Great Dane, Scooby-Doo, reunite to solve the mystery of ghostly happenings at the tropical resort Spooky Island. From a script co-written by James Gunn and featuring Rowan Atkinson as the eccentric resort-owner, the film was a box office success on its release and continues to have an avid following.

Director Yeon Sang-ho, whose prior filmmaking comprises groundbreaking animated features, balances an upbeat, kinetic energy with solid emotional storytelling to deliver much more than just an action-driven genre film.

Yeong-gyu, who cannot see, is a renowned wooden seal carver, respected for his intricate craftsmanship. Dong-hwan has no memory of his mother, who has been missing for 40 years—or so he’s been told—until he receives a startling call about her remains. Adapted from his own graphic novel, Yeon excavates the ugly aspects of societal standards and perceptions of beauty, and unapologetically exhibits the dark sides of human greed, desire, and trauma.

After the killing of Israeli hostages at the 1972 Summer Olympics in Munich, a Mossad agent (Eric Bana) assembles a team to assassinate the men deemed responsible for the murders. Steven Spielberg’s fact-based international thriller is a thoughtful look at the moral costs of violence, with gripping suspense and an impressive supporting cast including Best Actor winner Geoffrey Rush (Shine, 1996), Supporting Actor nominee Ciarán Hinds (Belfast, 2021), and Daniel Craig, shortly before he debuted as James Bond. The film received five Oscar nominations including Best Picture, Directing, and, for John Williams’ music, his 22nd feature score for the director. Williams’s somber, restrained score focused on, in the composer’s words, “the enormous suffering and guilt, and eventually, paranoia” of Bana’s protagonist.

Ponyo focuses on the friendship between 5-year-old Sosuke and a magical goldfish named Brunhilde, the young daughter of a sorcerer father and a sea-goddess mother. Now renamed Ponyo, she forms a quick bond with Sosuke that fuels her yearning to be a real girl, and together they shoulder the cost of what that might take. Rinko Tatsumi (Asuka Kurosawa) is a suicide hotline worker resigned to a life of unhappiness until she receives a package from a blackmailer. Through the increasingly vulgar acts of exhibitionism her blackmailer forces upon her, she learns to shed the social restrictions and repression dominating her life. Shot on black-and-white film and tinted a monochromatic blue, Shinya Tsukamoto’s A Snake of June is a visual feast. Filled with shaky, hand-held camerawork, voyeuristic close-ups, and near-constant rain, Tsukamoto creates a damp and cold erotic thriller that explores sexual dynamics, transformation, and releasing one's inner desires.

item.title: Marilyn & Me with Lawrence Schiller Book Signing and Conversation — Aug 20
item.description:

Thursday, August 20, 2026 at 6 pm
Location: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
Type: Book Signings
In a pre-signing conversation about Marilyn & Me, the author shares his personal account of photographing Monroe during the production of her unfinished final film, Something's Got to Give (1962). The book offers an intimate portrait of the actress in the final months of her life, alongside Schiller's recollections of the moments they shared.

When the family of Civil War veteran Ethan Edwards (John Wayne) is killed in a Comanche raid, he spends years looking for his kidnapped niece—but her uncle may prove more of a threat than her abductors. It has been cited as a favorite by many filmmakers, including Francis Ford Coppola, Martin Scorsese and Steven Spielberg, and has influenced films as diverse as Star Wars (1977) and Hardcore (1979). Three-time Oscar winner Winton C. Hoch (The Quiet Man, 1952) shot the film in VistaVision on stunning outdoor locations, including Monument Valley, culminating in a powerful, frequently imitated final image.

Hitchcock plays with the concept of the wrong man, a frequent theme in his narratives, in one of the most admired and entertaining of his mid-career films. North by Northwest stars four-time collaborator Grant as Roger O. Thornhill, a suave ad executive whose identity is mistaken for a government agent. Ruthless spy Philip Vandamm (James Mason) is after Thornhill; on a separate mission is a group of secret agents who follows Thornhill across the country. The second film from Dena Enterprises, the production company founded by actor Danny Kaye (White Christmas, 1954) and his songwriter wife, Sylvia Fine, The Court Jester is a delightful vehicle for the comedic icon to showcase his unparalleled timing, physical humor, and witty wordplay. Kaye is Hubert Hawkins, a retired carnival performer who disguises himself as a jester to help overturn an evil plot against a rightful British king. The most expensive comedy ever made at the time, primarily for its lavish sets, The Court Jester earned Kaye a Golden Globe nomination, and in 2004, the National Film Registry added the film to its list of titles considered “culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant.”

This gritty biopic dives into the smoky, dangerous glamor of Prohibition-era Chicago for the true story of nightclub performer Joe E. Lewis, famous for being one of the few people who could make gangster Al Capone laugh. Crooner Frank Sinatra, lauded by the film's marketing as “the most electric personality of our time,” follows Lewis’s highs and lows with the same realism and range he brought to The Man with the Golden Arm (1955). Ol’ Blue Eyes also adds musical dimension to the character — the real Lewis was more comedian than singer—with director Charles Vidor (no relation to fellow director King) compounding his experience with musicals and comedies into a story with dramatic nuance.

This zany romantic comedy was the fourteenth film to pair iconic comic duo Dean Martin and Jerry Lewis, released a year before their professional breakup. Martin plays Rick, a struggling painter, and Lewis is his roommate, Eugene, who is obsessed with a comic book character called Bat Lady. They become entangled with Bat Lady’s creator (Dorothy Malone) and her roommate/model (Shirley MacLaine) in a farcical plot that manages to incorporate government secrets and enemy spies. Frank Tashlin’s background in animation made him the perfect choice to direct this cartoon-infused romp, and he would collaborate often with Lewis after the split with Martin.

Four veterans return to the jungles of Vietnam in hopes of recovering a buried fortune in director/co-writer Spike Lee’s epic adventure drama, which pays homage to the classic The Treasure of the Sierra Madre (a favorite of the filmmaker’s) while exploring the rarely told experiences of Black soldiers in the Vietnam War. Fast-talking Rosalind Russell (His Girl Friday, 1940) is absolutely captivating as Kim Halliday, the daughter of a deceased career gambler who joins her father’s former business partner to run a Vegas casino. Russell's unflappable confidence is a fine match for the swagger of Fernando Lamas as Victor Monte, a rival club owner who vies for Kim’s affections—and her casino. There’s nothing quite like the neon lights of Sin City captured in high-definition VistaVision and vibrant Technicolor, which appear here in gorgeous documentary footage of the Strip; like most studio productions of the era, however, the bulk of this musical comedy was shot on producer Paramount’s lot.

Marlon Brando took on his only feature directing project—following the last-minute departure of original director Stanley Kubrick—with this character-oriented Western about a bank robber who tracks down a friend (frequent Brando co-star Karl Malden) who betrayed him. The Academy Award–nominated VistaVision color cinematography by Charles Lang Jr. (How the West Was Won,1962) makes strong use of scenic locations in Mexico and California, with vivid imagery of Brando riding his horse along the Monterey coastline. Until 2024, One-Eyed Jacks was the final film shot with the VistaVision process.
